q: What is the minimum age to serve as President under the Constitution?
why: Article II, Section 1 requires the President to be at least 35 years old.

q: What is the minimum age to serve as a U.S. Senator?
why: Article I, Section 3 requires Senators to be at least 30 and citizens for nine years.

q: What is the minimum age to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives?
why: Article I, Section 2 requires Representatives to be at least 25 and citizens for seven years.

q: How long is a U.S. Senator's term?
why: Article I, Section 3 provides six-year terms for Senators.

q: As originally written, who chose U.S. Senators?
why: The original Article I, Section 3 had Senators chosen by state legislatures; the 17th Amendment changed this.

q: How many witnesses to the same overt act does the Constitution require to convict for treason, absent a confession in open court?
why: Article III, Section 3 requires two witnesses to the same overt act or a confession in open court.

q: In which Article and Section does the Habeas Corpus Clause appear?
why: Article I, Section 9 bars suspending habeas corpus except in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it.

q: Under what conditions may the writ of habeas corpus be suspended?
choices: In cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it
why: Article I, Section 9 limits suspension to rebellion or invasion when the public safety may require it.

q: Which Article of the Constitution says no religious test shall ever be required for public office?
why: Article VI provides that no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification to any office or public trust.

q: How many state ratifying conventions did Article VII require to establish the Constitution among the ratifying states?
why: Article VII made ratification by nine state conventions sufficient.

q: What fraction of the states must ratify a constitutional amendment?
why: Article V requires ratification by three-fourths of the states.

q: Which Article of the Constitution establishes the federal judiciary?
why: Article III vests the judicial power in one Supreme Court and inferior courts Congress establishes.

q: Who serves as President of the Senate under the Constitution?
why: Article I, Section 3 makes the Vice President President of the Senate, voting only to break ties.

q: Who presides when the President is tried on impeachment in the Senate?
why: Article I, Section 3 provides that the Chief Justice presides when the President is tried.

q: Which branch does the Constitution give the power to declare war?
why: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to declare war.

q: Which Article contains the Supremacy Clause?
why: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties the supreme Law of the Land.

q: What are the first three words of the Constitution's Preamble?
why: The Preamble begins "We the People of the United States."

q: Where does the Constitution prohibit Congress from passing bills of attainder or ex post facto laws?
why: Article I, Section 9 bars Congress from passing them; Section 10 applies the same bar to the states.

q: On what day of September 1787 was the Constitution signed?
why: The Constitution was signed in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787.

q: Where did the Federal Convention of 1787 meet?
why: The Federal Convention convened in the State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia.

q: Which amendment protects the right of the people to keep and bear arms?
why: The Second Amendment protects the right of the people to keep and bear arms.

q: Which amendment bars quartering soldiers in a house in peacetime without the owner's consent?
why: The Third Amendment limits quartering of soldiers in private homes.

q: Which amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures?
why: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and requires probable cause for warrants.

q: Which amendment contains the protection against double jeopardy?
why: The Fifth Amendment says no person shall be twice put in jeopardy for the same offense.

q: Which amendment requires just compensation when private property is taken for public use?
why: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause requires just compensation.

q: Which amendment guarantees the accused the assistance of counsel?
why: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the assistance of counsel in criminal prosecutions.

q: The Seventh Amendment preserves civil jury trial in suits where the value in controversy exceeds what amount?
why: The Seventh Amendment applies to suits at common law over twenty dollars.

q: Which amendment prohibits excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments?
why: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

q: Which amendment says the enumeration of certain rights shall not be construed to deny others retained by the people?
why: The Ninth Amendment protects unenumerated rights retained by the people.

q: Which amendment reserves powers not delegated to the United States to the States or the people?
why: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the States or to the people.

q: Which amendment requires a grand jury indictment for capital or otherwise infamous federal crimes?
why: The Fifth Amendment's Grand Jury Clause covers capital or otherwise infamous crimes, with military exceptions.

q: Which amendment protects the right to petition the government for a redress of grievances?
why: The First Amendment protects speech, press, assembly, and petition, along with religious liberty.

q: How many amendments did the First Congress propose to the states in 1789?
why: Congress proposed 12 amendments; ten were ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights.

q: On what date was the Bill of Rights ratified?
why: Ten amendments were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on December 15, 1791.

q: One of the 12 amendments proposed in 1789 was finally ratified in 1992. Which amendment did it become?
why: The congressional pay amendment proposed in 1789 was ratified May 7, 1992 as the 27th Amendment.

q: Where was the First Congress held when it proposed the Bill of Rights?
why: The resolution begins: Congress of the United States begun and held at the City of New-York.

q: Which amendment abolished slavery?
why: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for crime.

q: Which amendment contains the Equal Protection Clause?
why: Section 1 of the Fourteenth Amendment bars states from denying any person equal protection of the laws.

q: In what year was the Fourteenth Amendment ratified?
why: The National Archives lists ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment on July 9, 1868.

q: Which amendment bars denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude?
why: The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified February 3, 1870.

q: Which amendment provides for direct popular election of U.S. Senators?
why: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified April 8, 1913, provides for direct election of Senators.

q: Which amendment bars denying the right to vote on account of sex?
why: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified August 18, 1920.

q: Which amendment repealed the Eighteenth Amendment's national Prohibition?
why: The Twenty-first Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the Eighteenth.

q: Under the Twentieth Amendment, presidential terms end at noon on what date?
why: The Twentieth Amendment ends the terms of the President and Vice President at noon on January 20.

q: Which amendment says no person shall be elected President more than twice?
why: The Twenty-second Amendment was ratified February 27, 1951.

q: Which amendment gave the District of Columbia electors in presidential elections?
why: The Twenty-third Amendment was ratified March 29, 1961.

q: Which amendment bars poll taxes as a condition of voting in federal elections?
why: The Twenty-fourth Amendment was ratified January 23, 1964.

q: Which amendment addresses presidential disability and filling a vice presidential vacancy?
why: The Twenty-fifth Amendment was ratified February 10, 1967.

q: Which amendment set the voting age at 18?
why: The Twenty-sixth Amendment was ratified July 1, 1971.

q: Which amendment delays any change in congressional pay until after an intervening House election?
why: The Twenty-seventh Amendment was ratified May 7, 1992.

q: Which amendment allowed Congress to tax incomes without apportionment among the states?
why: The Sixteenth Amendment was ratified February 3, 1913.

q: Which amendment requires electors to cast separate ballots for President and Vice President?
why: The Twelfth Amendment was ratified June 15, 1804.

q: Which amendment limits federal judicial power over suits against a state by citizens of another state or a foreign country?
why: The Eleventh Amendment was ratified February 7, 1795.

q: On what date did the Continental Congress adopt the Lee Resolution declaring independence?
why: Lee introduced it June 7; Congress adopted it July 2, 1776, with 12 of 13 colonies in favor.

q: When did most members of Congress sign the engrossed Declaration of Independence?
why: The Declaration was adopted July 4, 1776, but most members signed the parchment on August 2, 1776.

q: Which state's ratification on March 1, 1781 brought the Articles of Confederation into effect?
why: The Congress of the Confederation came into being when Maryland ratified on March 1, 1781.

q: Who introduced the resolution for independence in the Continental Congress in June 1776?
why: Richard Henry Lee of Virginia introduced the Lee Resolution on June 7, 1776.

q: What event on April 19, 1775 began the armed conflict of the Revolution?
why: The Battles of Lexington and Concord were fought April 19, 1775.

q: Which treaty, signed September 3, 1783, ended the Revolutionary War?
why: The Treaty of Paris was signed September 3, 1783.

q: Which federal statute's Section 1 is the origin of today's Section 1983 civil rights action?
why: The Act of April 20, 1871 enforced the Fourteenth Amendment; its Section 1 created the under-color-of-law civil action.

q: The Civil Rights Act of 1871 was titled an Act to enforce which amendment?
why: Its title reads: An Act to enforce the Provisions of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.

q: Which President signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
why: Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act on July 2, 1964 and the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965.

q: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on what date?
why: The Preliminary Proclamation issued September 22, 1862; the final Proclamation took effect January 1, 1863.

q: Which case established the federal courts' power of judicial review?
why: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established the courts' power to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.

q: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) held the Fifth Amendment's takings provision limited which government?
why: The Court held the provision is solely a limitation on the government of the United States.
case: Barron v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 32 U.S. (7 Pet.) 243 (1833)

q: Which 2008 case held the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a firearm unconnected with militia service?
why: Heller was decided June 26, 2008.
case: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)

q: Which case held the Second Amendment right recognized in Heller applies to the States?
why: McDonald was decided June 28, 2010.
case: McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)

q: NYSRPA v. Bruen (2022) concerned which New York licensing requirement?
choices: A "proper cause" requirement for public carry
A ban on handguns in the home
why: The Court held New York's proper-cause requirement violated the Fourteenth Amendment by preventing law-abiding citizens with ordinary self-defense needs from carrying in public.
case: New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)

q: What weapon was at issue in Caetano v. Massachusetts (2016)?
why: The per curiam vacated a ruling upholding a stun gun ban because its reasoning conflicted with Heller.

q: In United States v. Rahimi (2024), the Court upheld temporarily disarming a person found by a court to pose what?
choices: A credible threat to the physical safety of another
why: The Court held such a person may be temporarily disarmed consistent with the Second Amendment.

q: Garland v. Cargill (2024) held ATF exceeded its authority by classifying which device as a machinegun?
why: The Court held ATF exceeded its statutory authority by classifying a bump stock as a machinegun under 26 U.S.C. 5845(b).

q: United States v. Miller (1939) involved what type of firearm?
choices: A shotgun with a barrel under 18 inches
why: The Court said it could not take judicial notice that such a shotgun had a reasonable relation to a well regulated militia.

q: Presser v. Illinois (1886) described the Second Amendment as a limitation on whose power at that time?
why: Presser said the Amendment limited only the power of Congress and the national government, not the States.

q: United States v. Lopez (1995) struck down which federal law as beyond Congress's Commerce Clause power?
why: The Court held the Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded Congress's Commerce Clause authority.

q: Printz v. United States (1997) struck down a Brady Act provision commanding whom to conduct background checks?
why: The Court held the interim Brady Act provisions commanding local chief law enforcement officers to conduct background checks unconstitutional.

q: NRA v. Vullo (2024) was decided under which constitutional provision?
why: The Court held the NRA plausibly alleged a state official violated the First Amendment by coercing regulated entities to cut ties.
case: National Rifle Assn. of America v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)

q: Smith & Wesson v. Mexico (2025) held which federal statute barred Mexico's lawsuit?
choices: Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act
why: The Court held the PLCAA bars the suit because Mexico did not plausibly allege aiding and abetting.
case: Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc. v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280 (2025)

q: Which case held evidence from unconstitutional searches inadmissible in state criminal trials?
why: Mapp v. Ohio was decided June 19, 1961.

q: Weeks v. United States (1914), a foundational exclusionary rule case, was decided on which date?
why: The Library of Congress copy shows: Decided February 24, 1914.

q: Terry v. Ohio (1968) allowed what limited police action?
choices: A limited frisk for weapons of a person reasonably believed armed and dangerous
why: Terry allowed a limited frisk for weapons when specific facts lead an officer to reasonably conclude the person may be armed and dangerous.

q: Which case required procedural safeguards before statements from custodial interrogation may be used?
why: Miranda v. Arizona was decided June 13, 1966.

q: Vega v. Tekoh (2022) held that a violation of the Miranda rules does what?
choices: Does not by itself provide a basis for a Section 1983 claim
why: The Court held a violation of the Miranda rules does not provide a basis for a Section 1983 claim.

q: Brady v. Maryland (1963) concerns what prosecutorial duty?
choices: Disclosing material evidence favorable to the accused
why: Suppression of material evidence favorable to an accused, on request, violates due process regardless of good or bad faith.

q: Strickland v. Washington (1984) set a two-part test for what kind of claim?
why: A defendant must show deficient performance and prejudice.

q: Which case held the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees a jury trial in state criminal cases that would qualify under the Sixth Amendment?
why: Duncan v. Louisiana was decided May 20, 1968.

q: Chimel v. California (1969) limited a search incident to arrest to what area?
choices: The arrestee's person and the area within his reach
Any room the arrestee entered that day
why: The Court held searching beyond the arrestee and area within reach requires a warrant absent an exception.

q: Arizona v. Gant (2009) addressed searches of what?
choices: A vehicle's passenger compartment incident to a recent occupant's arrest
why: Police may search the compartment only if the arrestee could access it or it reasonably may contain evidence of the offense of arrest.

q: Kyllo v. United States (2001) involved what surveillance device used on a home?
why: Using a device not in general public use to explore details of a home is a search, presumptively unreasonable without a warrant.

q: United States v. Jones (2012) held that attaching what to a vehicle and monitoring it is a search?
why: The Government's attachment of a GPS device and its use to monitor the vehicle's movements is a Fourth Amendment search.

q: Florida v. Jardines (2013) held a drug-dog investigation at what location was a search?
why: The investigation of Jardines' home was a search within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

q: Riley v. California (2014) concerned warrantless searches of what?
choices: Digital data on an arrestee's cell phone
why: Police generally may not, without a warrant, search digital information on a cell phone seized from an arrestee.

q: Carpenter v. United States (2018) held acquiring what records is a Fourth Amendment search?
why: The Government's acquisition of Carpenter's cell-site records was a Fourth Amendment search.

q: Torres v. Madrid (2021) held that applying physical force with intent to restrain is a seizure even if what?
choices: The person does not submit and is not subdued
why: The Court held such force is a seizure even if the person does not submit and is not subdued.

q: Caniglia v. Strom (2021) rejected extending which doctrine to warrantless searches of the home?
why: The Court held neither the holding nor logic of Cady justifies such warrantless searches and seizures in the home.

q: Lange v. California (2021) held that pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does what?
choices: Does not categorically justify warrantless home entry
Requires a warrant in every case
why: Pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does not always, categorically, justify a warrantless home entry.

q: Under Tennessee v. Garner (1985), deadly force may not be used to prevent a suspect's escape unless the officer has probable cause the suspect poses what?
choices: A significant threat of death or serious physical injury
why: Garner required necessity plus probable cause of a significant threat of death or serious physical injury.

q: Under Graham v. Connor (1989), excessive force claims arising from an arrest or stop are analyzed under what standard?
why: Graham held such claims are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard.

q: Monell (1978) held local governments may be sued under 42 U.S.C. 1983, overruling in part which earlier case?
why: Monell overruled Monroe v. Pape insofar as it held local governments wholly immune from suit under Section 1983. Liability requires a policy or custom, not just employing the officer.
case: Monell v. Dept. of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

q: Bivens (1971) recognized a damages action against federal agents for violating which amendment?
why: Bivens held the complaint stated a federal cause of action under the Fourth Amendment for damages.
case: Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)

q: Pearson v. Callahan (2009) held the Saucier qualified immunity procedure is what?
why: The Court held the Saucier two-step procedure should not be regarded as an inflexible requirement.

q: Hope v. Pelzer (2002) involved what prison practice?
why: The Court held guards were not entitled to qualified immunity for the hitching-post treatment.

q: Taylor v. Riojas (2020) held officers were not entitled to qualified immunity because the conditions were so obviously what?
why: Any reasonable officer should have realized the conditions of confinement offended the Constitution.

q: Nieves v. Bartlett (2019) held a retaliatory arrest claim failed as a matter of law because of what?
why: Because there was probable cause to arrest Bartlett, his retaliatory arrest claim failed as a matter of law.

q: In Gonzalez v. Trevino (2024), what kind of evidence did the Court say was permissible to satisfy the Nieves exception?
choices: Objective evidence such as a survey of similar conduct
No evidence; the exception was abolished
why: The Court said demanding virtually identical comparators goes too far and that Gonzalez's survey was a permissible type of evidence.

q: Thompson v. Clark (2022) held a Fourth Amendment malicious prosecution plaintiff need not show what?
choices: That the prosecution ended with an affirmative indication of innocence
That the officer acted under color of law
why: The Court held a plaintiff need not show that the criminal prosecution ended with some affirmative indication of innocence.

q: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) requires a public official suing for libel over official conduct to prove what?
why: The official must prove the statement was made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of whether it was false.
case: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)

q: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) protects advocacy of force unless it is directed to inciting what?
choices: Imminent lawless action, and is likely to produce it
why: Brandenburg limited punishable advocacy to incitement of imminent lawless action likely to occur.

q: Texas v. Johnson (1989) concerned a conviction for what conduct?
why: The Court held Johnson's Texas flag desecration conviction inconsistent with the First Amendment.

q: West Virginia v. Barnette (1943) held unconstitutional a compulsory what?
choices: Flag salute and pledge in public schools
why: Compulsory flag salute and pledge for public school children violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments.
case: West Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624 (1943)

q: Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942) is known for describing which category of speech?
why: Chaplinsky described insulting or fighting words that tend to incite an immediate breach of the peace.

q: Near v. Minnesota (1931) is a landmark case on what First Amendment doctrine?
why: The Court held the statute unconstitutional as applied to publications charging official neglect and corruption.

q: Snyder v. Phelps (2011) held the First Amendment shielded Westboro Baptist Church from liability for what?
why: The Court held the First Amendment shields Westboro from tort liability for its picketing in that case.

q: Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988) involved what kind of publication?
choices: A political cartoon in a newspaper
why: Public figures may not recover emotional distress damages for a parody like the ad without a false statement of fact made with actual malice.
case: Hustler Magazine, Inc. v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988)

q: Cohen v. California (1971) reversed a conviction for wearing what?
why: The Court held the State could not make the simple public display of that four-letter expletive, in those circumstances, a criminal offense.

q: United States v. Eichman (1990) concerned prosecution under which law?
why: Prosecution for burning a flag in violation of the federal Act was held inconsistent with the First Amendment.

q: NAACP v. Alabama (1958) protected the NAACP from compelled disclosure of what?
why: The Court protected the membership lists, citing the chilling effect on freedom of association.
case: NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, 357 U.S. 449 (1958)

q: Reno v. ACLU (1997) held provisions of which statute abridged the freedom of speech?
why: The CDA's indecent transmission and patently offensive display provisions abridged the freedom of speech.
case: Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union, 521 U.S. 844 (1997)

q: Mahanoy Area School District v. B. L. (2021) involved what kind of student speech?
why: The school's interests were not sufficient to overcome B. L.'s interest in free expression in that case.
case: Mahanoy Area School Dist. v. B. L., 594 U.S. 180 (2021)

q: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) involved a public school coach's what?
why: The Court held the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses protected his private religious expression.
case: Kennedy v. Bremerton School Dist., 597 U.S. 507 (2022)

q: Which case held racial segregation in public schools violates the Equal Protection Clause?
why: Brown v. Board of Education was decided May 17, 1954.
case: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)

q: In what year was Plessy v. Ferguson decided?
why: Plessy was decided May 18, 1896.

q: Which amendment's Citizenship Clause overruled Dred Scott v. Sandford's holding that Black Americans could not be citizens?
why: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens, overruling that part of Dred Scott.
case: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857)

q: Smith v. Allwright (1944) concerned exclusion of Black voters from which state's Democratic primary?
why: The Court held the exclusion was state action violating the Fifteenth Amendment and overruled Grovey v. Townsend.

q: Sweatt v. Painter (1950) required admission to which school?
why: The Court held equal protection required the petitioner's admission to the University of Texas Law School.

q: Hernandez v. Texas (1954) held unconstitutional the exclusion of jurors on what basis?
why: The Court held exclusion of jurors because of ancestry or national origin violates the Fourteenth Amendment.

q: On what date was the Texas Declaration of Independence adopted?
why: The Convention of 1836 adopted the Declaration on March 2, 1836.

q: Where did the Convention of 1836 meet to declare Texas independence?
why: The Convention met at Washington-on-the-Brazos beginning March 1, 1836.

q: Who chaired the committee that drafted the Texas Declaration of Independence?
why: George C. Childress was chairman of the drafting committee.

q: How many delegates signed the Texas Declaration of Independence?
why: The Handbook of Texas reports fifty-nine delegates signed it.

q: What was the first battle of the Texas Revolution, fought over a cannon?
why: The Gonzales "Come and Take It" fight on October 2, 1835 is considered the first battle of the Texas Revolution.

q: What words appeared on the flag at Gonzales in 1835?
why: The flag bore an image of a cannon and the words "Come and Take It."

q: In what year had the Mexican government given the cannon to the Gonzales colonists?
why: The cannon was loaned to Gonzales in 1831 on condition it could be reclaimed.

q: To whom was William B. Travis's famous February 24, 1836 Alamo letter addressed?
choices: The People of Texas and All Americans in the World
why: Travis addressed it To the People of Texas and All Americans in the World and vowed Victory or Death.

q: On what date did Mexican forces launch the final assault on the Alamo?
why: The siege began February 23; the final assault came March 6, 1836.

q: The Goliad Massacre occurred on which day?
why: At sunrise on Palm Sunday, March 27, 1836, Fannin's men were executed.

q: About how long did the Battle of San Jacinto last?
why: The Handbook of Texas states the battle lasted but eighteen minutes.

q: What were the Texan battle cries at San Jacinto?
choices: Remember the Alamo! and Remember Goliad!
why: Texan forces charged crying Remember the Alamo! and Remember Goliad!

q: At Velasco on May 14, 1836, Santa Anna signed how many treaties?
choices: Two, one public and one secret
why: Texas officials had Santa Anna sign two treaties, one public and one secret.

q: Who took the oath as president of the Republic of Texas on October 22, 1836?
why: Sam Houston took the oath before a joint session of Congress on October 22, 1836.

q: Where did the First Congress of the Republic of Texas assemble in October 1836?
why: The First Texas Congress assembled at Columbia on October 3, 1836.

q: Who was the last president of the Republic of Texas, who declared "the Republic of Texas is no more"?
why: Anson Jones spoke those words at the February 19, 1846 transfer ceremony.

q: On what date did Texas legally enter the Union?
why: The Handbook calls December 29, 1845 the date of Texas's legal entry into the Union.

q: By what vote did the July 1845 Texas convention approve annexation?
why: The delegates approved annexation 55 to 1; Richard Bache of Galveston dissented.

q: Which Union general issued General Order No. 3 at Galveston on June 19, 1865?
why: Gen. Gordon Granger's order informed Texans that all slaves are free.

q: In what year did Juneteenth become an official Texas state holiday?
why: The Handbook of Texas reports the bill by Rep. Al Edwards became law in 1979.

q: On what date did Texas voters ratify the current Texas Constitution?
why: Voters ratified the Constitution of 1876 on February 15, 1876, 136,606 to 56,652.

q: The Texas Constitution of 1876 was the state's which constitution since independence from Mexico?
why: TSHA describes it as the state's sixth constitution since independence.

q: When did the Texas Firearm Carry Act (HB 1927), allowing eligible adults to carry a handgun without a license, take effect?
why: Texas DPS states the Firearm Carry Act took effect September 1, 2021.

q: Texas concealed handgun licenses issued under 1995's Senate Bill 60 became effective on what date?
why: SB 60 took effect September 1, 1995, but licenses issued before January 1, 1996 were not effective until that date.

q: Which section of Article I of the Texas Constitution protects the right to keep and bear arms?
why: Art. I, Sec. 23 protects the right to keep and bear arms in the lawful defense of oneself or the State.

q: Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 23 gives the Legislature power to regulate what?
choices: The wearing of arms, with a view to prevent crime
why: Sec. 23 allows the Legislature by law to regulate the wearing of arms, with a view to prevent crime.

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights covers searches and seizures?
why: Art. I, Sec. 9 protects persons, houses, papers and possessions from unreasonable seizures or searches.

q: Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 9 protects persons, houses, papers and what?
why: The Texas text says possessions, where the federal Fourth Amendment says effects.

q: Which section of Article I of the Texas Constitution says the writ of habeas corpus shall never be suspended?
why: Art. I, Sec. 12: The writ of Habeas Corpus is a writ of right, and shall never be suspended.

q: Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 13 bars cruel OR unusual punishment. How does that differ from the Eighth Amendment?
choices: The Eighth Amendment says cruel AND unusual
why: Texas uses "cruel or unusual," while the federal text says "cruel and unusual."

q: Which Texas Bill of Rights section contains the open courts and due course of law remedy guarantee?
why: Art. I, Sec. 13 says all courts shall be open and every person shall have remedy by due course of law.

q: Under Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 19, no citizen may be deprived of life, liberty or property except by what?
choices: Due course of the law of the land
why: Art. I, Sec. 19 uses the phrase "due course of the law of the land."

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights declares everything in it excepted from the general powers of government and forever inviolate?
why: Art. I, Sec. 29 declares the Bill of Rights excepted out of the general powers of government.

q: Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 1 says Texas is a free and independent State subject only to what?
choices: The Constitution of the United States
why: Sec. 1 says Texas is subject only to the Constitution of the United States.

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights protects free speech and the press?
why: Art. I, Sec. 8 says every person shall be at liberty to speak, write or publish his opinions on any subject.

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights protects the right to assemble and petition?
why: Art. I, Sec. 27 protects peaceable assembly and petition for redress of grievances.

q: Which section of Article I of the Texas Constitution protects the right to hunt, fish, and harvest wildlife?
why: Art. I, Sec. 34 protects the right to hunt, fish, and harvest wildlife, subject to conservation laws.

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights contains the protection against double jeopardy?
why: Art. I, Sec. 14 is headed Double Jeopardy.

q: Which section of the Texas Bill of Rights prohibits imprisonment for debt?
why: Art. I, Sec. 18 is headed Imprisonment for Debt.

q: Texas Constitution Art. I, Sec. 6 declares a natural and indefeasible right to do what?
choices: Worship Almighty God according to the dictates of conscience
why: Sec. 6 protects the right to worship Almighty God according to the dictates of one's own conscience.

q: Which article of the Texas Constitution is its Bill of Rights?
why: The Texas Bill of Rights is Article 1 of the Texas Constitution.
